title: Public S3 bucket exposed with public-read-write access and no encryption
description: The Pulumi IaC creates an S3 bucket configured with ACL set to public-read-write, which effectively makes all objects in the bucket readable and writable by anyone on the internet. The snippet also lacks any encryption or versioning configuration, increasing the risk of data exposure, tampering, and data loss without recoverability. Public access in combination with force_destroy further raises risk by enabling destructive actions by any actor. This pattern can lead to sensitive data leakage, data integrity issues, and potential use as a staging area for malicious uploads.
suggested_fix: Change bucket ACL from public-read-write to private or use a restrictive bucket policy that grants access only to intended principals. Enable server-side encryption (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS) and enable bucket versioning to retain previous object versions. Remove force_destroy or protect final deletion (MFA Delete) as applicable. Consider using bucket policies or IAM roles to tightly control access and disable public access at the account level with Block Public Access settings.
snippet:
bucket = aws.s3.Bucket(
    "public-data-bucket",
    acl="public-read-write",  # VULNERABILITY: Public access
    force_destroy=True,
    # VULNERABILITY: No encryption, no versioning
)

title: RDS instance publicly accessible with storage encryption disabled and weak admin password
description: The Pulumi IaC defines an RDS instance with storage_encrypted set to false and publicly_accessible set to true, meaning the database is exposed to the public internet and its data at rest is not encrypted. Additionally, the admin password is set to a weak value (password123). This combination creates a severe risk of unauthenticated access, data exfiltration, and data compromise. Public database exposure significantly broadens the attack surface and can lead to unauthorized administrative access if credentials are exposed or guessed.
suggested_fix: Enable encryption at rest by setting storage_encrypted to true (and use a KMS key if needed). Disable public accessibility (set publicly_accessible to false) and place the database in a private network/subnet with proper firewall rules. Use a strong, unique admin password and store credentials securely (e.g., in AWS Secrets Manager) rather than hard-coding in IaC. Implement database security controls (TLS connections, rotating credentials, and network ACLs).
snippet:
database = aws.rds.Instance(
    "database",
    engine="mysql",
    engine_version="5.7",
    instance_class="db.t2.micro",
    allocated_storage=20,
    storage_encrypted=False,  # VULNERABILITY: No encryption
    publicly_accessible=True,  # VULNERABILITY: Public access
    db_name="mydb",
    username="admin",
    password="password123",  # VULNERABILITY: Weak password
    skip_final_snapshot=True,
)
